findings.claim: FlexPrefill's accuracy is not uniformly preserved relative to full attention; on some models and tasks it degrades, notably Yi and several InfiniteBench retrieval tasks.
findings.mechanism: Sparse index selection with a cumulative-attention threshold can omit tokens that matter for particular retrieval or multi-key tasks. The paper does not analyze why these cases fail, so the cause remains unexplained.
conditions: Yi-9B-200K on RULER and InfiniteBench
Retr.KV and Retr.Number tasks
gamma set to 0.9 or 0.95

evidence.support_description: Llama Retr.KV drops from 60.00 (full attention) to 44.00. Yi Retr.KV drops from 29.00 to 24.00, Retr.Number from 99.66 to 91.53, and average from 37.69 to 36.18.
Yi RULER average is 76.32 versus 79.49 for full attention, with 128k at 56.97 versus 66.35.

caveats: Gains over full attention on other models (e.g., Qwen, Llama on RULER) suggest the effect is model-dependent.
Differences on small benchmark subsets may be partly noise.

findings.claim: The speed/accuracy trade-off depends on gamma, which must be tuned per model, and aggressive sparsity sharply degrades long-context quality.
findings.mechanism: Lowering gamma reduces the attention mass covered and therefore the computed budget. This speeds up processing but loses information, especially at 128k. Different models need different gamma values (0.9 or 0.95), so the adaptive method still has a manually chosen hyperparameter.
conditions: Low gamma (≤0.85)
Context lengths of 64k-128k
Model-specific gamma and tau selection

evidence.support_description: For Llama-3.1, 128k score falls from 79.09 at gamma=0.95 to 74.28 at 0.85 and 62.02 at 0.6, and the average falls from 89.18 to 83.25.
gamma is set to 0.9 for Yi and Qwen and 0.95 for the other models.

caveats: The authors present gamma as a controllable knob for balancing speed and quality.

findings.claim: The method depends on a minimum budget and on keeping the first and last key blocks, which suggests the adaptive selection is unreliable for heads with extreme sparsity.
findings.mechanism: With smaller gamma, some heads select too few tokens and malfunction. A hard minimum budget of 1024 tokens is therefore needed as a workaround. The underlying cause is not analyzed.
conditions: gamma ≤ 0.9
No minimum-budget constraint

evidence.support_description: Llama at gamma=0.9 without a minimum budget scores 84.78 versus 88.38 with 1024; GLM scores 85.26 versus 88.58.
The first and last key blocks are always retained and each head computes at least 1024 tokens.

caveats: The minimum budget is unnecessary at high gamma (0.95).

findings.claim: Sparse index selection for Vertical-Slash heads, and the pattern decision, rely on a single representative query block (the last block), which can fail when that block is unrepresentative.
findings.mechanism: Vertical and slash line importance is estimated only from the last block_size queries and extrapolated to all queries. Using other query positions yields poor estimates.
conditions: Vertical-Slash heads
Representative queries not at the sequence end

evidence.support_description: Using the middle query block for vertical-slash index selection collapses average RULER performance from 89.18 to 38.18.

caveats: The last-block choice is tuned and works in the reported setup.
Whether tasks where the final query block is unrepresentative are affected is not examined.

findings.claim: The query-aware/vertical-slash decision is sensitive to tau, and an inappropriate threshold degrades performance.
findings.mechanism: Too large a tau lets heads with inaccurate pooled attention estimates be classified as Query-Aware. The Jensen-Shannon divergence is computed only on the last query block, so it is a proxy for estimation quality over all queries.
conditions: Llama at 128k

evidence.support_description: Llama 128k drops from 79.09 at tau=0.1 to 75.96 at tau=0.3. The text notes that too large a tau degrades performance.
The best tau varies slightly by model, yet tau is fixed at 0.1 for all models.

caveats: The effect of tau is small for several models; Table 6 differences are around 1 point or less.

findings.claim: Efficiency and accuracy gains are demonstrated only on a limited set of models and benchmarks, mostly synthetic, and with GPU latency measured for the attention operation rather than end-to-end.
findings.mechanism: Evaluation uses four 7-9B models on RULER and InfiniteBench with one A100 GPU. Speedups are for attention latency during prefill only. Overheads from pattern search and index construction are measured in isolation, and short contexts incur higher non-attention overheads.
conditions: Models of 7-9B parameters
Synthetic or retrieval-style benchmarks
Prefill phase only; decoding stays dense
Short contexts

evidence.support_description: All baselines use dense decoding. At shorter input lengths, non-attention computation overheads are higher.
Latency is for a single attention call, not end-to-end.

caveats: Appendix D adds comparisons on additional baselines and another model (Llama-3-8B-262k).

findings.claim: The theoretical rationale for cumulative-attention selection is loose and does not cover the block-pooled, estimated approximation actually used.
findings.mechanism: The error bound (1−a_S)Σ|v_j| is derived for exact per-query attention. The implementation uses pooled block estimates, a global flattened threshold across queries, and a vertical-slash extension, none of which are covered by the guarantee. The duality argument is also loose (relaxed LP, equivalence to a threshold).
conditions: Query-Aware heads using pooled Q/K
Global flatten selection
Vertical-Slash extension from a subset of queries

evidence.support_description: The bound is per query position with exact attention scores, whereas Algorithm 4 thresholds pooled block scores flattened over the whole map.

caveats: The authors show empirically that the flattened and per-query variants perform similarly (Table 9).

findings.claim: The accuracy and efficiency claims compare against baselines at unequal operating points. FlexPosit needs 4.1–5.0 b to match BitMoD's 4 b PPL. Qwen2.5-14B needs 5.0 b, and LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B need 4.6 b. The 'sub-5-bit near-FP16' claim is therefore weaker for larger or harder models, and the 'matches group-wise accuracy' claim holds only at a higher bit budget.
findings.mechanism: Per-channel Posit(4,1) with power-of-two scaling leaves a residual accuracy gap to group-wise 4-bit quantization. The gap is closed only by spending extra bits on sensitive windows. The required budget p* rises with model size.
conditions: Iso-PPL matching against BitMoD 4 b
Larger or more heavy-tailed models (Qwen2.5-14B, LLaMA-2-7B, Mistral-7B)

evidence.location: Table II; Sec. VI-B 'Quantization comparison'; Fig. 9
evidence.support_description: PEB precision ranges from 4.1 b to 5.0 b, and Qwen2.5-14B needs 5.0 b. The text states p* shifts higher for larger models.

caveats: The trend is based on a few models; larger models (>14B) were not evaluated.
At 4.1 b, mean ΔPPL is still 0.64 versus BitMoD's 0.40.

findings.claim: Sensitivity profiling is expensive and calibration-dependent. It requires one full-model perplexity evaluation per channel window, and the same dataset (WikiText-2) is used for profiling and for reporting perplexity. Generalization of the allocation to other data or tasks is not tested, and the profiling cost is not reported.
findings.mechanism: Algorithm 2 re-evaluates end-to-end PPL after upgrading each individual window. The cost therefore scales with the number of windows times the evaluation cost. The allocation is tuned to the PPL signal on the evaluation dataset, which risks overfitting to the metric.
conditions: Large models with many channel windows
Use of the same dataset for profiling and evaluation

evidence.location: Sec. IV-B, Algorithm 2; Sec. VI-A; Table III; Fig. 10
evidence.support_description: Fisher-ranked allocation is a cheaper proxy but is clearly worse than the PPL-profiled allocation, which indicates a cost/accuracy trade-off. No profiling cost is reported.

caveats: The paper does not state whether profiling and evaluation data are held out from each other.
The downstream MMLU and HellaSwag results partly mitigate this concern.

findings.claim: The evaluation scope is narrow. It is weight-only quantization with FP16 activations; the FP8-activation test covers only perplexity on three models. There is no KV-cache or attention quantization, and accuracy is mainly WikiText-2 perplexity plus two downstream benchmarks. Models are at most 14B, so the claims may not extend to larger LLMs, to W4A4 regimes, or to other tasks.
findings.mechanism: Only weights are encoded as SerialPosit. All arithmetic is done in FP16 (or FP8 in one test), so the compute-side benefits of low-precision activations are not realized or evaluated.
conditions: Weight-only quantization
Models up to 14B parameters
Perplexity-centric evaluation

evidence.location: Sec. IV-A; Sec. VI-A; Table V; Table VI

caveats: Weight-only is argued to dominate edge inference memory.
The activation precision limitation is acknowledged implicitly by comparing OliVe, which uses W/A 4 b or 8 b, against FlexPosit's FP16 activations.

findings.claim: The hardware results come from synthesis and a cycle-level simulator rather than a fabricated or full-system implementation. The baselines are re-scaled from other technology nodes using generic process factors. Comparisons are iso-area on a small 32×16 array with a mostly compute-only area budget. The reported advantages could be sensitive to the modeling assumptions and the scaling.
findings.mechanism: PE area and power come from 16 nm synthesis of FlexPosit. BitMoD, OliVe and FP16 numbers are scaled to 16 nm using standard factors. The system model is a simulator with CACTI and Ramulator, and the iso-area constraint covers compute only.
conditions: Iso-area at a 32×16 array
Scaled baseline area and power
Batch size 1 and sequence length 256 by default

evidence.location: Sec. VI-A 'Hardware Implementation' and 'Iso-area and Iso-PPL Evaluation Setup'; Table VII

caveats: Table X shows the advantages shrink with larger batch and sequence length (speedup over OliVe falls from 1.5× to 1.2×).
Only one array size is evaluated.

findings.claim: The bit-serial design pays a latency and throughput cost for higher precision. Latency grows nearly linearly with bit-width, and the 4-way PE grouping only compensates at the 4 b minimum. FlexPosit supports only 4–8 bit weights, so lower-bit (2–3 b) regimes are not covered. Utilization also depends on batch/activation parallelism: four activations per weight are needed to fill each cluster.
findings.mechanism: Each cluster delivers 4/P MACs per cycle, so throughput matches FP16 MAC rate only at P=4. Larger P reduces throughput proportionally. The cluster design requires four distinct activations per decoded weight term.
conditions: Precision above 4 b
Workloads with limited activation parallelism

evidence.support_description: Latency increases nearly linearly with precision, and the advantage over baselines shrinks at larger batch/sequence length.

caveats: Gains at the largest workload remain positive.
The paper does not evaluate the utilization of the four-way clusters under real LLM decode workloads.

findings.claim: Channel-window granularity and the power-of-two scale restrict flexibility. Precision is set per window of 256 (1024 for Qwen) channels, a granularity chosen per model. The scale is restricted to a power of two with a 4 b index, which sacrifices the calibrated real-valued scaling that group-wise methods use. SerialPosit also gives up encoded-domain operations and fixes es=1 for all models.
findings.mechanism: Hardware alignment to the array columns forces coarse windows and shared scaling. A power-of-two scale can align the distribution only coarsely with the Posit profile. The fixed es=1 was chosen empirically for low-bit regimes.
conditions: Hardware alignment to systolic array column count
Fixed es=1

evidence.location: Sec. IV-A; Sec. IV-B; Sec. VI-A 'Quantization Setup'; Sec. V-C

caveats: Ablation (Table IV) shows channel-window MPQ beats layer-wise MPQ.
No ablation of window size or of power-of-two versus real-valued scales is reported.

findings.claim: The reasons for FlexPosit's accuracy gains are only partly established. The attribution to Posit's tapered precision aligning with weight distributions is supported by perplexity comparisons rather than by isolating the mechanism. Some inconsistencies and confounds also remain. Comparisons with OliVe use a different quantization (W/A 4/8 b) and omit some model entries. The claim of why p* grows with model size is speculative.
findings.mechanism: The paper claims that Posit's tapered precision matches heavy-tailed weights and that larger models need more precision because they are more heavy-tailed. No direct analysis or controlled experiment isolates the cause beyond the INT4/E2M1/Posit comparison on one model.
conditions: Comparison with INT4/FP4 on Qwen2.5-7B only (Fig. 3)
Cross-model trend of p*

evidence.location: Sec. III-B; Fig. 3; Fig. 4; Sec. VI-B 'Precision scalability trends'
evidence.support_description: The explanation that larger, more heavy-tailed LLMs require higher precision is stated without supporting analysis.

caveats: Table II marks several OliVe entries as unavailable ('–'), so those comparisons are incomplete.

findings.claim: Hybrid prioritization depends on a manually tuned interpolation parameter alpha. A single value does not work across loads: large alpha penalizes long requests, and small alpha is less effective under overload.
findings.mechanism: Alpha weights SRPF-like length preference against EDF deadline ordering. Higher alpha lowers median latency but deprioritizes long requests, so the best value depends on load. The authors use an offline sweep for fixed QPS and a load-adaptive switch for variable QPS (alpha=1 at low load, alpha=8 at high load), which needs load knowledge and per-deployment tuning.
conditions: Fixed-QPS runs use an offline alpha sweep from 0 to 10 to minimize SLO violations
Variable-QPS runs need load-adaptive tuning of alpha
Fairness to long requests degrades as alpha increases

evidence.support_description: Alpha is a configurable hyperparameter chosen by offline sweep and adapted by load; a larger alpha means violated deadlines for most long requests.

caveats: No automatic, principled mechanism for choosing alpha is presented
Robustness of alpha to different workloads and SLO mixes is not shown

findings.claim: Priority for non-interactive requests relies on an over-approximated decode length (historical mean plus two standard deviations per application) because true decode length is unknown. The approximation may be inaccurate for applications with no history or with heavy-tailed or shifting output lengths.
findings.mechanism: Eq. 5 needs the remaining decode time. QoServe substitutes a per-application historical estimate, justified by the assumption that TTLT deadlines are much larger than processing time. Errors in this estimate distort priority ordering and violation prediction.
conditions: Non-interactive requests (TTLT SLOs)
The TTLT deadline is not much greater than the true processing time
Application output-length distribution is non-stationary or lacks history

evidence.support_description: Decode length is unknown, so a two-standard-deviation over-approximation from historical data is used, backed only by the claim that it is sufficient (§4.4.1).

caveats: Sensitivity to the decode-length estimate is not evaluated
The Azure Code trace has very short decodes (p50 of 8 tokens), which may mask estimation error

findings.claim: Dynamic chunking gains are limited under PD disaggregation, where chunk sizes are already large, and in the decode nodes. Different TBT SLOs on decode nodes are not supported.
findings.mechanism: Dynamic chunking exploits slack by growing chunks above the small chunk size forced by TBT. In disaggregated prefill nodes the default chunk is already 8K and unconstrained by TBT, so only prioritization and relegation help. Decode nodes use a fixed maximum batch size sized for the strictest TBT, so diverse TBT tiers there are left to future work.
conditions: PD disaggregated deployments
Multiple distinct TBT SLOs on decode nodes

evidence.support_description: Gains are lower than in PD colocation because dynamic chunking cannot be exploited; efficiently supporting different TBT SLOs in decode nodes is left to future work.

caveats: Disaggregated results use only the Az-conv trace and the artifact reproduces only Llama3-8B

findings.claim: Dynamic chunking relies on a learned batch-latency predictor profiled per model, hardware, and parallelism configuration. It carries up to 10% error in chunk size and is deliberately biased to under-predict, so it can leave throughput unrealized.
findings.mechanism: A random forest is trained on profiles from the Vidur simulator harness for each configuration. Prediction errors force conservative under-prediction to avoid latency violations, and new models, hardware, or parallelism settings require new profiling.
conditions: A new model, hardware, or parallelism configuration requires fresh profiling
Predictor error margin up to 10% on chunk size

evidence.support_description: The random forest is trained per configuration and the prediction error is under 10%; it is tuned to under-predict, which may scarcely miss fully maximizing throughput.

caveats: No sensitivity analysis of predictor error on SLO attainment is given

findings.claim: The evaluation is narrow. QoServe uses only three synthetic QoS tiers and trace-derived workloads on single-GPU or small-TP replicas, with Poisson arrivals and random assignment of requests to tiers and priorities. The cluster-scale result is a single 16-GPU Llama3-8B Azure Code run, and the headline 23% saving comes from a coarse capacity-estimated silo baseline. Generalization to production multi-tenant settings is unproven.
findings.mechanism: Requests are randomly split into tiers and priority labels independent of their length or content. Arrivals are Poisson and the diurnal pattern is compressed from a weekly cycle into 4 hours. The silo baseline is sized from per-replica throughput estimates and round-robin balancing. Real correlations between application, request length, and priority are not captured.
conditions: Cluster-scale evaluation on Llama3-8B with the Azure Code trace only
Three equally split tiers (also two skewed mixes tested at one load)
Random 20% low-priority tagging

evidence.location: Section 4 (Workloads and QoS Tiers); Section 4.1.1, Table 4; Section 4.3
evidence.support_description: Tiers are assigned by dividing the datasets into equal parts, priorities are random, and the load pattern is compressed.

caveats: The artifact appendix notes reproductions use fewer requests and a coarser sweep than the paper

findings.claim: Graceful degradation under overload relies on application-provided priority hints and on relegating requests, which causes violations or very high latency for the relegated ones. The relegated requests are served only opportunistically and can see latencies of thousands of seconds.
findings.mechanism: When requests are predicted to miss their deadlines, they are moved to a relegated queue and served only under lower load. Protection of important requests depends on accurate free/paid hints. Without hints, high-priority requests are also relegated once no low-priority ones remain.
conditions: Sustained or extreme overload
Accurate application hints on request importance
Relegated requests tolerate delayed service

evidence.support_description: QoServe still misses deadlines for 8.64% of all requests, and relegated requests saw a maximum latency of up to 3900s.

caveats: Eager relegation depends on the violation checker's predictions, whose accuracy is not separately evaluated
The relegation fraction needed grows with overload

findings.claim: Comparisons with concurrent systems (Medha, PolyServe, SLOs-Serve) are limited. They are best-effort reimplementations without autoscaling or migration, and SLOs-Serve is compared only qualitatively.
findings.mechanism: The concurrent systems are not open-source, so the authors re-implement only core policies in their own framework, using synthetic traces or simplified setups. Gains may not reflect the original systems' full capabilities.
conditions: Medha comparison on a synthetic trace (10K prefill, 500 decode tokens) at a very low goodput of 0.32 vs 0.26 QPS
PolyServe comparison omits autoscaling and request migration
SLOs-Serve has no empirical comparison
caveats: Medha's own benefit appears only for long prompts, so the median-length datasets do not exercise it

findings.claim: Selective preemption restricts QoServe. It never preempts decode-phase requests, and preempts prefill requests only if this causes no violation, to limit KV-cache memory overhead. This limits flexibility, and long non-interactive prefills in progress can still hold KV memory and block urgent work.
findings.mechanism: Decodes are never preempted because TBT targets are strict, and partially prefilled requests retain KV cache. Memory pressure from preempted prefills is avoided by restriction rather than quantified.
conditions: Large KV caches from long prompts
Memory-constrained GPUs

evidence.support_description: Preemption is allowed only for requests in the prefill queue and only if it does not lead to a deadline violation.

caveats: The memory impact of preemption is not measured

findings.claim: Tessera's overlap gains depend on the workload's compute-to-communication ratio. Workloads with short expert GEMMs relative to A2A time (e.g., Qwen3-Next-M) still expose a large share of EP communication.
findings.mechanism: Fewer parameters per expert give shorter GEMM durations relative to A2A transfer time. Each overlap pair then has too little computation to hide the A2A latency, so inter-microbatch overlap cannot hide it.
conditions: Models with small per-expert compute relative to A2A volume
Extremely sparse MoE (TopK=10/512) with small expert size

evidence.support_description: On the 5,120-GPU Qwen3-Next-M run, steady-phase exposed EP is 18.2% of iteration time. Only 26% of EP communication is hidden and total exposed EP is 38.9%, versus 73% hidden for Qwen3-Next-L.

caveats: The authors attribute the cause to compute intensity but do not run an ablation that isolates it
The two workloads differ in cluster size and other factors

findings.claim: Even in the favorable regime, a significant fraction of EP communication stays exposed and pipeline bubbles remain, so the method leaves a gap to ideal execution.
findings.mechanism: Warmup and cooldown phases of interleaved 1F1B cannot be overlapped by the inter-microbatch scheme. Residual stage imbalance also persists.
conditions: Interleaved 1F1B fixed as the schedule template
Qwen3-Next-L at 8,192 GPUs

evidence.support_description: 27% of EP communication remains exposed (819 ms), over 40% of it from warmup/cooldown. PP bubbles add 8.5% (835 ms), and exposed EP plus pipeline idle together are 17% of iteration time.

caveats: The authors state they are targeting this in ongoing optimization

findings.claim: The static planner's cost model does not match real hardware, and the cheaper primitive-level profiling alternative is unreliable for partition selection. Chunk-pair profiling on real hardware is therefore required.
findings.mechanism: SM contention (~20 SMs reserved for A2A), coarse task granularity and cross-primitive effects (relay overlaps, cache/communication-library state, host launch overhead) cause deviations from the idealized task-DAG schedule. The MILP relies on relative cost comparisons, so a few misestimated pairs can change the chosen bottleneck edge or partition boundary.
conditions: Using analytical or primitive-composed cost estimates instead of ground-truth profiling
Chunk-pair profiling needs a dedicated reference device group with the same TP/EP topology

evidence.location: §5 Theoretical Overlap vs. Silicon Reality; Granularity of Cost Profiling
evidence.support_description: Theoretical cost underestimates measured cost by ~5% on average, with a stable 10–20% slowdown from SM contention. Primitive-level profiling errors reach up to 15% in tail cases.

caveats: Profiling stays under one hour at the reported scales, so it is affordable for the tested workloads

findings.claim: The partitioner searches only a bounded neighborhood around a serial-balanced baseline and uses a max-edge surrogate objective, so the chosen partition is not guaranteed globally optimal for the true iteration time.
findings.mechanism: Candidates are generated by perturbing boundaries around the baseline to keep profiling tractable. The MILP minimizes the maximum steady-state post-overlap edge cost rather than the full critical path. Pruning discards any pair costing more than the baseline's bottleneck, so Tessera cannot do worse than the baseline's bottleneck but also cannot find distant better partitions.
conditions: Pipeline schedule template fixed in advance (e.g., interleaved 1F1B)
Candidate neighborhood K is bounded

evidence.support_description: The text says candidates are restricted to a bounded neighborhood and that the maximum post-overlap edge cost is used as a surrogate objective.

caveats: No evaluation compares the result to an unrestricted search or to full critical-path optimization

findings.claim: The Dynamic Bubble Optimizer trades memory for throughput and its benefit is limited by the bounded movable-task pool. Aggressive bubble filling can cause OOM on memory-constrained workloads.
findings.mechanism: Deferring Wgrad tasks prolongs the liveness of activations and gradients, raising peak memory. The pool is therefore capped by a per-GPU limit and available headroom, which limits the bubble filling that can be done.
conditions: Memory-constrained workloads
Pool cap must be tuned by hand from observed memory headroom

evidence.support_description: Aggressive bubble filling occasionally triggered OOM in production. DBO raises peak memory by 2–4 percentage points of the per-GPU budget.

caveats: The reported DBO runtime gains are modest, 4.4–5.4% in the ablation and 3.4% on the 6,144-GPU run
The memory-management-as-movable-task mitigation is described but not evaluated

findings.claim: Tessera is only demonstrated for routing-induced bubbles; handling infrastructure jitter (network congestion, switch contention) at 10K+ GPU scale is unvalidated.
findings.mechanism: Jitter bubbles are proposed to be predicted with a moving-average history predictor feeding the same DBO injection path. This has not been systematically tested under controlled jitter.
conditions: Large-scale clusters with network noise

evidence.support_description: The authors state that systematic validation of this extension remains future work.

caveats: The extension is described as architecturally feasible only

findings.claim: The evidence for the headline gains is mostly production-only and compares against an internal baseline, with limited controlled public comparisons. This limits attribution and reproducibility.
findings.mechanism: The 20–33% gains are measured against an internal Megatron fork on proprietary models and clusters. The component breakdown comes from a single phased 'hot upgrade' trace on one job, and the Qwen3-Next-M comparison uses different GPU counts across experiments. Against public Megatron-Core recipes, the gain is significant only for Qwen3-235B, and Tessera is merely comparable on the non-Qwen models, which the paper also reports as 'comparable' rather than superior.
conditions: Proprietary models (Qwen3-L/XL, Qwen3-Next-M/L/XL), datasets and cluster
Gains over open-source recipes were tested only on 256 GPUs and three models

evidence.support_description: The baseline is an internal Megatron fork. Against Megatron-Core MoE, Tessera is 1.24× on Qwen3-235B and 'comparable' on the non-Qwen models.

caveats: Baseline MFU for the Qwen3-Next models is low because of immature optimizations, which may inflate relative gains
Phase 1 gains are partly attributed to unspecified 'latency hiding' without a clean ablation

findings.claim: Tessera depends on a fixed pipeline schedule template, manual instrumentation of model code, and a specific host framework, which restricts generality.
findings.mechanism: The planner co-optimizes only within a given template such as interleaved 1F1B and does not choose the schedule. Task boundaries must be exposed through probes (advance/register_task) inserted into forward/backward code, and Tessera is implemented as a plug-in only for Megatron-LM. Interleaved 1F1B also needs padding with shadow actions when the microbatch count is not divisible by the pipeline size.
conditions: Models whose operators are manually annotated with task probes
Megatron-LM host framework
Interleaved 1F1B-style templates

evidence.support_description: The design fixes the high-level schedule. Probes are inserted in existing code, and microbatch padding adds ~0.5% overhead.

caveats: The authors report that custom schedules can be specified through YAML

findings.claim: Heuristic overlap scheduling is validated only against a time-limited ILP reference, so its optimality gap is not established.
findings.mechanism: The ILP solved with CBC under a 300-s budget often does not prove optimality, so '~1% of ILP' compares against an unproven reference. +DEFER adds only modest mean gain over +ALIGN.
conditions: Evaluation on Qwen3-Next-M at 4K sequence length, EP8/EP32

evidence.support_description: Many instances hit the 300-s budget without proven optimum. +DEFER's mean gain over +ALIGN is modest.

caveats: The heuristic is within ~1% of the ILP reference on measured post-overlap cost

insufficient_evidence_reason: CalledProcessError: Command '['<python>', '-m', 'pipeline.limitset_baselines', '_case', 'b1', '<project-root>/out/limitset2/b1_sonnet/runs/LS2-05/r1/input', '<project-root>/out/limitset2/b1_sonnet/runs/LS2-05/r1', '1']' returned non-zero exit status 1.; see generator.log

findings.claim: Chunked prefills make prefill computation less efficient than unchunked prefills. This raises prefill cost and TTFT, and the effect grows as chunks get smaller (tighter TBT SLOs).
findings.mechanism: Each chunk's attention re-reads the KV-cache of all earlier chunks from HBM. Smaller chunks also lower GPU utilization and add fixed kernel-launch overheads. Tile quantization can inflate prefill time further for chunk sizes that are not tile-aligned.
conditions: Strict TBT SLOs that force small token budgets (e.g., 512)
Long prompts split into many chunks
Chunk sizes misaligned with GPU tile sizes

evidence.support_description: Overhead is up to ~25% for chunk size 512 and near zero at 2048. A chunk size of 257 can raise prefill time by 32% over 256.
Chunked-prefills-only raises P50 TTFT (1.04s vs 0.53s on openchat_sharegpt4; 5.38s vs 3.78s on arxiv_summarization) relative to hybrid-batching-only.
The authors acknowledge that chunked prefills are slower than full prefills and that disaggregated approaches can yield better TTFT.

caveats: The overhead is described as moderate, and the paper's evaluation emphasizes P99 TBT and capacity.
Overhead was measured only for Yi-34B, though the authors say trends are consistent across model-hardware combinations.

findings.claim: Sarathi-Serve needs a token budget tuned per SLO, model, parallelism configuration and hardware. The paper uses fixed budgets and leaves dynamic adaptation to workload changes unexplored.
findings.mechanism: The best token budget depends on competing factors: TBT SLO, chunking overhead, tile quantization, and pipeline bubble variance. The paper resolves this with one-time offline profiling or simulation (Vidur) for a given deployment, not an adaptive policy.
conditions: Changes in SLO, model, hardware, parallelism or workload characteristics
Pipeline-parallel deployments, where larger chunks increase bubbles

evidence.support_description: Calls token budget selection 'a complex decision' that depends on SLO, parallelism and hardware, and uses one-time profiling and Vidur.
Uses fixed budgets of 2048 (relaxed) and 512 (strict), with 1536 for LLaMA2-70B relaxed. Dynamic variation based on workload is left for future work.

caveats: The authors present this tunability as an advantage for controlling the tradeoff.
The reliance on profiling and simulation may be a practical burden when deployments or workloads change.

findings.claim: The reported capacity gains come from a limited evaluation scope. It covers four models, two datasets, a Poisson arrival process, P99 TBT SLOs derived from decode times, and only vLLM and Orca as baselines. Generalization to other workloads, systems and metrics is not shown.
findings.mechanism: The evaluation uses synthetic Poisson arrivals over request-length distributions from two datasets, with outliers removed (length caps of 8192 and 16384). It defines capacity under TBT SLOs plus a 2s median scheduling delay limit. The Orca baseline is the authors' own implementation. Disaggregated systems such as Splitwise and DistServe are not compared quantitatively.
conditions: Workloads with short prompts, bursty traffic or different length distributions
Comparison against disaggregated serving, or models with different architectures
TTFT-sensitive applications

evidence.support_description: Poisson arrivals, two datasets with long outliers filtered, median TTFT and P99 TBT as metrics.
'We leave a quantitative comparison between Sarathi-Serve and disaggregation-based solutions for future work.'
All four evaluated models use GQA, and only A100 and A40 GPUs are tested.

caveats: The authors claim generality across models, hardware and parallelism strategies.
The headline gains are the maximum across settings and vary widely, e.g., 1.65x to 6.3x.

findings.claim: The paper does not fully explain why Sarathi-Serve's gains in pipeline-parallel settings are so large. It does not isolate how much comes from bubble reduction versus the stall-free scheduling benefit, and the baselines may be weak.
findings.mechanism: The PP gains (up to 5.6x) are attributed to 'few pipeline bubbles' from uniform batches, but bubble time is not directly measured or broken down. The vLLM PP baseline is the authors' own pipeline-parallel implementation. The claim that bubbles are the cause relies on capacity comparisons and an illustrative 4k-prompt example.
conditions: Pipeline-parallel deployments (TP4-PP2 over Ethernet)
Comparison against the authors' own PP implementation of vLLM and Orca

evidence.support_description: Attributes the gains to fewer bubbles, but reports only end-to-end capacity numbers and no direct bubble measurement.
Bubble size is estimated with a single Falcon-180B example (~950 ms).

caveats: Figure 8 and Figure 13 offer qualitative and indirect support for the bubble explanation.
The ablation in Table 4 covers only Yi-34B on TP-2, not the PP setting.

findings.claim: Sarathi-Serve is a research prototype without full feature parity with vLLM, and it was tested only on specific hardware and software.
findings.mechanism: The implementation was adapted from a vLLM fork for research iteration, retaining only critical features. It relies on FlashAttention-2 and FlashInfer kernels for paged chunked prefill and was tested with CUDA 12.1 on A100 and A40 GPUs.
conditions: Production deployments needing the full vLLM feature set
Other GPU types or software stacks

evidence.support_description: States it is a research prototype without complete feature parity, and was tested with CUDA 12.1 on A100 and A40 GPUs.
Chunked prefill depends on FlashAttention v2 and FlashInfer kernels, and the FlashAttention backend was used for all evaluations.

caveats: The source code is open and has been used by other work.

findings.claim: StreamingLLM does not extend the context window or long-term memory; the model can only use information inside its current cache (sink tokens plus recent window), so it is unsuitable for tasks needing long-range dependencies such as long-document QA and summarization.
findings.mechanism: Tokens evicted from the rolling KV cache are permanently discarded, so the model cannot attend to them. Information outside the cache is lost regardless of the sink tokens.
conditions: Tasks where the needed information lies beyond the cache size
Long-document QA, summarization, and other long-term-memory tasks

evidence.location: Appendix A Limitations; Appendix C, Table 7
evidence.support_description: On StreamEval, accuracy falls to 0.00 once the query-answer token distance exceeds the cache size (e.g., 100 lines/2300 tokens with a 4+2044 cache). Accuracy also degrades as the distance grows within the cache.

caveats: The authors present this as a design scope rather than a flaw; the method is meant for short-term-memory streaming use.
StreamingLLM can be combined with context-extended models to enlarge the cache.

findings.claim: On long-input benchmarks, StreamingLLM with 4 sink tokens plus recent tokens underperforms the standard truncation baseline, because it drops initial prompt content.
findings.mechanism: Evicting the middle and early input removes crucial prompt or task information. Only 4 initial tokens are kept, rather than the 1750 initial tokens the truncation baseline retains.
conditions: Tasks where the beginning of the input carries critical information, such as instructions or documents
LongBench tasks with Llama-2-7B-chat and a 3500-token budget

evidence.support_description: StreamingLLM 4+3496 scores below truncation on all six tasks. For example, NarrativeQA is 11.6 vs 18.7 and GovReport is 23.9 vs 27.3. Performance recovers only when 1750 initial tokens are kept.

caveats: The attribution to loss of initial prompt information is stated as 'likely' and is not directly tested.
The comparison covers one model and a 3500-token budget.

findings.claim: Increasing the cache size does not consistently reduce perplexity, indicating the models do not effectively use the extra context, so StreamingLLM gains little from larger caches.
findings.mechanism: Perplexity is non-monotonic in cache size, and the paper only speculates that models fail to fully utilize extended context. No causal analysis is given.
conditions: Larger cache sizes on Falcon-7B, MPT-7B, Pythia-12B, and Llama-2-7B
Perplexity measured on 400K tokens of PG19

evidence.support_description: Llama-2-7B perplexity is 9.08 at 4+2044 but 9.59 at 4+4092. MPT-7B perplexity rises monotonically from 14.12 to 14.99 as the cache grows. Falcon-7B is 12.34 at 4+1020 and 12.84 at 4+2044.

caveats: The explanation is hypothesized, not verified.
Perplexity may not reflect downstream use of context.

findings.claim: Pre-trained models without a dedicated sink token need several (about four) initial tokens as sinks, and fewer sinks only partially restore performance. The cause is not established beyond a hypothesis, so the choice of 4 is an empirical heuristic.
findings.mechanism: The authors hypothesize that models spread sink behavior across multiple initial tokens because pre-training samples lack a consistent starting token. This is not directly verified for the pretrained models tested, and model-specific variation (e.g., Llama-2 vs Falcon/MPT) is unexplained.
conditions: Existing pretrained LLMs without a sink token
Using 1–2 sink tokens instead of 4

evidence.support_description: Llama-2-7B perplexity is 11.88 with 1 sink, 10.51 with 2, and 9.59 with 4. Falcon, MPT, and Pythia saturate at 1 sink token.

caveats: The explanation is a stated belief or hypothesis.
Four tokens work empirically across the tested models.

findings.claim: The pre-training sink-token benefit is validated only on small 160M-parameter models trained on one dataset. Its generality to larger LLMs is untested. Adding a second sink token gave no benefit.
findings.mechanism: The sink-token pre-training experiments use a single small Pythia-160M setup with a reduced batch size, and perplexity is evaluated on a single PG19 sample. Larger-scale behavior and how the approach interacts with other pre-training choices are unknown.
conditions: Pre-training from scratch with a sink token
Scaling beyond 160M parameters

evidence.location: Section 3.3, Section 4.2, Table 3, Appendix I Tables 9–10
evidence.support_description: Only 160M models were trained. Streaming perplexity is evaluated on the first PG19 sample. The second sink token gives no consistent benchmark gains, and the model depends on both sink tokens (perplexity 25.73 with 1+1023).

caveats: The sink-token models show similar downstream accuracy to vanilla, with differences within noise.
Existing off-the-shelf models cannot benefit without retraining.

findings.claim: The theoretical account of attention sinks is largely intuitive and speculative. The claim that attention sinks are a universal property of Transformers is supported only by limited qualitative evidence beyond decoder LLMs.
findings.mechanism: Attention sinks are explained via softmax normalization and initial-token visibility, backed mainly by attention-map visualizations. The Zero Sink (SoftMax1) experiment only partly alleviates the problem, which does not confirm the softmax explanation. Claims about BERT and ViT rest on one example plus a related paper.
conditions: Explaining why initial tokens become sinks
Extrapolating to encoder and vision Transformers

evidence.location: Section 3.1, Table 3, Appendix H, Appendix B
evidence.support_description: Zero Sink gives only partial improvement (0+1024 PPL 29214, needing other initial tokens). BERT evidence is a single sentence visualization, with the claim of universality stated as an assumption/contention.

caveats: Authors label the explanation as 'intuitive' and 'we hypothesize'.
Observations are consistent across several decoder LLMs.

findings.claim: StreamingLLM is demonstrated mainly with perplexity on concatenated PG19 books and synthetic or short-range QA streams; evidence of real long-running conversational quality is limited, and sequence-boundary effects confound the perplexity curves.
findings.mechanism: The 4M-token claim relies on perplexity over concatenated books, where perplexity fluctuates at book transitions. StreamEval is synthetic. The ARC streaming test concatenates independent questions that need little cross-question context. Stable perplexity does not show that the model retains useful long-horizon behavior.
conditions: Claims of stable modeling at 4M+ tokens
Real multi-round dialogue deployment

evidence.support_description: Figure 5 notes perplexity fluctuations due to book transitions. The ARC streaming comparison is against one-shot sample-by-sample prompting. StreamEval accuracy is shown only up to about 120K tokens.

caveats: Accuracy on streamed ARC matches the one-shot baseline.
Only the 'potentially more' claim is extrapolated beyond 4M tokens.

findings.claim: Efficiency is only compared against the sliding-window-with-recomputation baseline, in a single hardware and implementation setting. The up-to-22.2× speedup depends on cache size and is much smaller for large caches.
findings.mechanism: The speedup comes from avoiding recomputation, and it shrinks as the cache grows (about 2× at cache 4096 for Llama-2-7B vs 22.2× at 256). The comparison uses HuggingFace Transformers on one A6000 and does not benchmark against other KV-cache compression methods.
conditions: Large cache sizes
Different hardware, kernels, or serving stacks

evidence.support_description: For Llama-2-7B, the re-computation baseline takes 63 ms vs 31 ms at cache 4096, but 1411 ms vs 65 ms at cache 256. Memory use is about the same as the baseline.

caveats: The authors call re-computation the only baseline with acceptable quality.
Memory use is not reduced versus the baseline.

findings.claim: The theoretical guarantee for H2O depends on assuming the attention scheme is submodular, which is not verified empirically. The guarantee covers an idealized score function (h concave, monotone), whereas the implemented Algorithm 1 uses h(z)=z with plain accumulated attention.
findings.mechanism: Theorem 4.4 and Lemma 3.1 hold only 'under mild assumptions' (submodularity, universal monotone and dynamic conditions, bounded approximation error). The paper never tests these assumptions on real attention. The proof also uses a score function different from the one deployed, so the bound may not describe the practical algorithm.
conditions: Assumes attention is submodular and monotone
Assumes the universal dynamic conditions with parameters θ, γ and approximation error ε0
Score function h is concave in the analysis but identity in the implementation

evidence.location: Section 3.2 Lemma 3.1; Section 4.2 Theorem 4.4; Remark D.14
evidence.support_description: Results are stated informally under 'mild assumptions' and 'assuming the attention scheme is submodular'. Algorithm 1 uses h(z)=z for intuition, while the analysis uses concave h.

caveats: The paper presents the theory only as a heuristic explanation and as guidance for future work
The guarantee is stated per step with free parameters α and β

findings.claim: Accumulated-attention scoring is biased toward older tokens, and the proposed averaged-score fix degrades performance. The bias is therefore left unresolved.
findings.mechanism: Earlier tokens receive attention at more decoding steps, so their accumulated scores are larger and they are retained more often. Normalizing by the number of steps (averaged attention) was tried and performed worse. The cause is not analyzed.
conditions: Eviction based on summed attention scores

evidence.support_description: The authors note a bias favoring the least recent tokens and report that the averaged-score alternative degraded performance.

caveats: The size of the bias's practical effect is not quantified

findings.claim: Heavy-hitter behavior, and the observation that H2 correlates with word co-occurrence, is shown only on a limited set of models and data. The explanation for why H2 emerges is not established.
findings.mechanism: The correlation between accumulated attention and token co-occurrence (Fig. 2b) and the power-law claims come from visualizations on OPT-1.3B, OPT-6.7B and similar models. No causal analysis is given. The sparsity analysis uses a 1%-of-max threshold. The figures show vocabulary-index plots with no statistical test. The mechanism that makes recent plus heavy tokens sufficient is therefore not explained.
conditions: Observations made mainly on OPT with WikiText-103
Sparsity defined via a 1%-of-row-max threshold

evidence.support_description: Claims rest on qualitative plots and a correlation described as 'high', with no causal test.

caveats: Ablations do show that removing H2 hurts accuracy

findings.claim: Needed KV budget grows for short-sequence settings. Gains are not guaranteed at the headline 20% budget for all tasks.
findings.mechanism: In zero- and one-shot inference, sequences are short (about 100–300 tokens). Some tasks need 30–40% of the KV cache to match full-cache accuracy. The 5× reduction therefore depends on long prompts such as 5-shot.
conditions: Short prompts (0/1-shot)
Harder tasks needing more context information

evidence.support_description: The authors report that some zero/one-shot tasks require a higher KV budget of 30–40%.

caveats: Local-only baselines fail even more severely

findings.claim: Evictions are irreversible, so H2O can lose critical middle-context tokens, and it requires an equal split between heavy hitters and recent tokens. Neither the split nor the budget is adapted per task.
findings.mechanism: Evicted KV entries are never recoverable. Tokens that look unimportant at one decoding step may matter later. The budget is fixed and split evenly between heavy hitters and recent tokens, with no mechanism to adapt it. Per-head eviction also adds bookkeeping.
conditions: Fixed budget split between H2 and recent tokens
Tasks where relevance of tokens changes late in generation

evidence.support_description: Evicted KV embeddings become inaccessible in subsequent steps, and H2O evenly splits the budget between H2 and recent tokens.

caveats: Reported results show matching accuracy on the tested tasks

findings.claim: Evaluation scope is narrow. Accuracy is tested mostly on short multiple-choice or classification tasks with small models. Throughput claims are tied to a FlexGen/OPT implementation on specific GPUs, and the long-context benefits are demonstrated beyond OPT's trained length without quality validation.
findings.mechanism: Most accuracy results use COPA, PiQA, OpenBookQA, Winogrande and RTE with small test sets, and some differences are within a point or two. Summarization is evaluated on 1000 samples. Throughput is measured against baselines with synthetic padded prompts. H2O is implemented only on FlexGen and OPT. The paper benchmarks sequences up to 10K tokens even though OPT is trained on 2K, so those results demonstrate speed rather than quality.
conditions: Throughput numbers from FlexGen-based OPT implementation on T4/A100
Synthetic fixed-length prompts
Models evaluated beyond their training context

evidence.location: Section 5.2 Setup; Appendix A Experiment Details; Table 3, Table 5
evidence.support_description: Systems experiments use synthetic padded datasets and OPT, which the authors note is trained only on 2K sequences.

caveats: XSUM real-data throughput is also reported in Table 4

findings.claim: Combining H2O with quantization gives limited speedup in practice, and it adds overhead.
findings.mechanism: The FlexGen 4-bit quantization implementation has considerable computational overhead. Despite a 20× larger batch size, throughput improved by less than 2×.
conditions: FlexGen's unoptimized quantization kernels

evidence.support_description: The authors state that the throughput gain is less than 2× despite a 20× batch size increase.

caveats: The authors suggest optimized CUDA kernels could improve this

findings.claim: Quest does not reduce KV cache memory footprint; it only reduces memory bandwidth/movement during decoding. The full KV cache plus per-page min/max metadata must stay resident.
findings.mechanism: Quest retains all KV cache (no eviction) and adds per-page min and max Key vectors as extra metadata. Savings come only from loading Top-K pages instead of the whole cache, so capacity-bound deployments gain no memory relief and pay a small extra storage cost.
conditions: Settings where GPU memory capacity, not bandwidth, is the bottleneck
Long contexts whose full KV cache cannot fit on the device
caveats: The paper contrasts Quest favorably with eviction methods on accuracy, but does not report memory capacity usage
Metadata overhead is analyzed only as load cost (1/page size), not as capacity cost

evidence.support_description: Quest 'retains all of the KV cache'; criticality estimation loads min/max vectors of every page, about 2M*L/S bytes.

findings.claim: Quest is not lossless in general. Quest is not applied to the first two layers, and there is an accuracy-efficiency tradeoff governed by a hand-set budget K.
findings.mechanism: Early layers have low sparsity (<10%), so Quest and all baselines are skipped there and use the full cache. The Top-K page budget is an arbitrary hyperparameter that must be tuned per task, and overall sparsity is capped by the dense layers. Page-level selection also forces whole pages to be loaded, which can include non-critical tokens.
conditions: Models and tasks where more layers are dense or have low sparsity
Tasks needing broad attention such as summarization or aggregation, which require larger budgets
caveats: The authors state skipping the first two layers is orthogonal to the selection algorithm
Lossless sparsity on LongBench is only 1/5 to 1/10 after counting full-cache layers
No automatic, adaptive method for choosing K is given

evidence.support_description: K is described as 'an arbitrarily defined hyper-parameter'. Lossless results need budgets around 1K-5K and sparsity 1/5-1/10 on LongBench, and the first two layers are excluded.

findings.claim: The criticality estimate is an upper bound, which can be loose, so it may select pages incorrectly. The paper offers no theoretical guarantee on selection quality and no thorough ablation of page size.
findings.mechanism: The score sums per-channel max(q_i*m_i, q_i*M_i) independently across channels, so the bound need not be reachable by any actual key. A page with outlier channels can score high though none of its tokens attend strongly, and large pages loosen the bound. Why this bound ranks pages well is shown only empirically, via the oracle alignment in Fig. 3 and recall in Fig. 4.
conditions: Larger page sizes, where min/max span many tokens
Key distributions with outlier channels or high variance within a page
caveats: Empirical alignment with the oracle is shown only for LongChat-7B on PG19
Fig. 8 varies page size for kernel latency, but accuracy as a function of page size is not systematically analyzed

evidence.support_description: Per-channel upper bound summed over channels; validation is by empirical comparison with oracle sparsity and recall.

findings.claim: The evaluation is narrow: only two 7B Llama-2-based long-context models, six LongBench tasks, a single-batch setting, and a limited set of baselines. Generality to other architectures, larger models, and serving scenarios is untested.
findings.mechanism: Experiments use LongChat-7B-32k and Yarn-Llama-2-7B-128k with MHA (32 heads). LongBench accuracy uses only LongChat. Efficiency is measured on RTX4090/Ada 6000 with batch size 1. Models with GQA/MQA, MoE, or larger sizes are not tested, and batched serving is not tested, where per-request top-K selection may reduce memory-load savings and complicate batching.
conditions: GQA/MQA models, where KV heads are shared and the 16GB cache estimate and selection granularity differ
Batched or multi-request serving
Models above 7B or with different position encodings
caveats: The authors claim the memory-load reduction is universal across models, but only analytically
Yarn-128k is evaluated only on passkey retrieval

evidence.support_description: Two models; LongBench on LongChat only; end-to-end evaluated in 'real-world single-batch scenarios'.

findings.claim: The baseline comparisons are partly unfair or only qualitative, and the evaluation protocol favors Quest. This weakens claims of superiority.
findings.mechanism: Eviction baselines are evaluated in a setup where the question is fed token by token after prefill with full attention, which puts eviction methods at a disadvantage. H2O collects attention scores only from decoding because of FlashAttention. Baseline efficiency is estimated from FlashInfer latency at the required budget, ignoring their overheads, whereas Quest is measured with a real implementation. Passkey retrieval is a simple task, and other query-aware or sparse-attention methods such as SparQ are not compared empirically.
conditions: Interpreting speedups over TOVA/H2O (3.8x-4.5x)
Comparing with query-aware methods such as SparQ
caveats: The authors acknowledge the baselines lack kernel implementations
Prefill is not sparsified, so Quest accelerates only decoding

evidence.support_description: Question fed token by token; H2O scores not collected during context stage; baseline latency 'qualitative analysis' disregarding runtime overheads; SparQ only discussed, not evaluated.

findings.claim: Speedups depend on long sequences and shrink or vanish at short lengths. End-to-end gains are much smaller than the headline kernel speedup and depend on hardware, weight quantization, and budget.
findings.mechanism: Quest adds overhead (criticality estimation, Top-K) and the attention fraction of decode time is limited. At short sequence lengths the estimation kernel underutilizes memory bandwidth. The 7.03x speedup applies only to the self-attention kernel at 32K with budget 2048. End-to-end speedup is 1.74x (FP16) or 2.23x (4-bit), and grows with context length.
conditions: Short contexts (e.g., a few thousand tokens)
Setups where attention is a small fraction of latency, such as FP16 weights with large FFN cost
caveats: Evaluation uses an RTX4090 for kernels and an Ada 6000 for end-to-end, so results may differ on other GPUs
Quest improves over FlashInfer at all tested lengths, with small gains at 8K

evidence.support_description: Estimation underutilizes bandwidth at short lengths; only 1.69x attention speedup at 8K; end-to-end 1.74x/2.23x at 32K.

findings.claim: Scaling salient channels only helps up to a point. Large scale factors raise the quantization step size for non-salient channels, so accuracy degrades and the best scale must be found by search.
findings.mechanism: Scaling a weight by s>1 can raise the group maximum and so the quantization step Δ'. This amplifies error in non-salient weights in the same group. In OPT-6.7B, Δ changes for 21.2% of groups at s=4, and the best perplexity is at s=2, not at larger s.
conditions: Per-input-channel scaling inside quantization groups (group size 128)
Large scale factors (e.g., s=4)
INT3 quantization on OPT-6.7B

evidence.support_description: PPL improves from 23.54 to 11.92 at s=2 but worsens to 12.36 at s=4 as the share of changed Δ rises to 21.2%.

caveats: Reported only for OPT-6.7B at INT3-g128
Equation 5 and the clipping step partly mitigate the effect

findings.claim: The scale search is a heuristic and not a direct optimization. It uses a one-parameter family s = s_X^α and a grid of 20 values. This may not find the optimal per-channel scales.
findings.mechanism: The quantizer is non-differentiable. The authors report that approximated-gradient (STE) optimization converged unstably, so they restrict scales to a function of average activation magnitude and do a grid search over a single α. Per-channel scales are not freely optimized, and saliency is assumed to depend only on mean activation magnitude.
conditions: Saliency is assumed to be determined by average per-channel activation magnitude
One α is shared across the layer's channels

evidence.support_description: They state that approximated gradients 'still suffer from unstable convergence' and that they use a simple search space with a grid of 20.

caveats: The paper does not compare against a more general optimization of the scales
The hypothesis that large-activation channels are important is stated but not proven

findings.claim: The error analysis rests on empirical approximations, so the claimed error reduction is not a rigorous guarantee. Because the salient-channel gain is argued from these approximations, it may not hold exactly in every case.
findings.mechanism: The derivation assumes the rounding error is unchanged at about 0.25 (uniform), that scaling one element leaves the group maximum unchanged (Δ'≈Δ), and that Δ and x carry no quantization error in FP16. These are 'empirically found' assumptions and not proofs. The paper itself notes that Δ' changes for a growing share of groups at larger s. It also only hypothesizes why activation magnitude indicates importance.
conditions: Small scale factors (s<2), where Δ'≈Δ holds for most groups

evidence.support_description: The text says 'We hypothesize that the input features with larger magnitudes are generally more important.' The approximations Δ'≈Δ and constant RoundErr are described as empirical findings.

caveats: Table 2 supports the trend for OPT-6.7B only

findings.claim: Quantization quality is not lossless at very low bit-widths. At INT3, and especially INT2, AWQ shows substantial degradation. INT2 needs GPTQ as an add-on and still leaves large gaps to FP16.
findings.mechanism: With very few quantization levels, scaling and clipping cannot fully compensate for the error. RTN fails at INT2, and AWQ alone is not reported at INT2. Combining with GPTQ is required to reach usable results. INT3 multimodal results (OpenFlamingo) still lose 7.23 CIDEr at 32-shot.
conditions: INT2 or INT3 weight quantization
Small models, e.g., OPT-1.3B

evidence.support_description: OPT-1.3B INT2-g64 perplexity is 35.71 with AWQ+GPTQ versus 14.62 for FP16. OpenFlamingo INT3 AWQ drops 7.23 CIDEr at 32-shot. OPT-1.3B INT3 AWQ is 16.32 versus 14.62 for FP16.

caveats: INT4-g128 is near-lossless in many reported settings
The INT2 setup uses group size 64, not 128

findings.claim: Weight-only quantization with W4A16 gives speedups only in the memory-bound, small-batch generation regime. The benefits for compute-bound or large-batch serving are not shown.
findings.mechanism: The speedup comes from reduced weight memory traffic at batch size 1. The context stage is compute-bound with arithmetic intensity ≥165. Activations stay in FP16 and weights are dequantized on the fly. Dequantization adds compute overhead (shift, AND and FMA per weight) and is costly on SIMD CPUs.
conditions: Batch size 1
Decoding-dominated on-device use
Short prompts (4 tokens in benchmarks)

evidence.support_description: The roofline analysis targets batch size 1. The speed benchmarks use batch size 1 with a fixed prompt length of 4 tokens.

caveats: The authors explicitly target on-device use cases
Throughput under batched or long-context serving is not evaluated

findings.claim: Some of the evidence for generalization is limited in scope. Efficacy is shown mainly through perplexity, a few small calibration-shift tests and qualitative examples. It is not shown across diverse models and calibration domains.
findings.mechanism: Primary evaluation is WikiText-2 perplexity on LLaMA and OPT. The robustness test uses only two calibration subsets (PubMed, Enron) on a single model, OPT-6.7B, at INT3. Instruction-tuned evaluation uses 80 questions scored by GPT-4. Only the language part of OpenFlamingo is quantized. Other model families such as BLOOM are excluded.
conditions: OPT-6.7B at INT3-g128 for the calibration-robustness results
Vicuna 7B/13B with the 80-question GPT-4 evaluation

evidence.support_description: BLOOM was omitted because it is 'generally worse in quality'. Calibration robustness is tested only on OPT-6.7B with two Pile subsets. The OpenFlamingo experiment quantizes only the language part.

caveats: Additional results on Mistral/Mixtral, VILA, MBPP and GSM8K broaden coverage

findings.claim: Some accuracy results are not uniformly better than baselines, so the claim of consistent superiority is overstated. Small drops against FP16 remain even at INT4, and AWQ is sometimes behind on certain metrics.
findings.mechanism: Quantization error remains after scaling. On MBPP, AWQ pass@10 (49.25) is below FP16 (49.77) and below RTN's 48.49 only slightly above. On GSM8K, AWQ is below FP16 for all sizes. On VILA, AWQ is lower than FP16 on several benchmarks (e.g., VizWiz 57.8 vs 59.6).
conditions: INT4-g128 quantization
Code, math and VLM benchmarks

evidence.support_description: VILA-7B VizWiz drops from 59.6 to 57.8. GSM8K-7B drops from 13.87 to 13.57. MBPP pass@10 is 49.25 versus 49.77 for FP16.

caveats: Differences are small and no variance or multiple seeds are reported

findings.claim: The system speedups depend on custom, platform-specific kernels and packing. The generality of the 3× speedup claim is limited by the hardware and baselines tested.
findings.mechanism: TinyChat needs hand-tuned fused kernels, platform-specific weight packing (ARM NEON, GPU interleaving) and graph lowering to C++ on CPUs. Reported speedups are relative to the HuggingFace FP16 implementation, which is slow for some models. Part of the gain comes from FP16 kernel fusion and not from quantization. Falcon's baseline had a KV-cache issue. The CPU packing gain is only up to 1.2×.
conditions: Specific GPUs (RTX 4090, 4070 laptop, Jetson Orin) and ARM CPU
Comparison with HuggingFace FP16

evidence.support_description: For Llama-2-7B, FP16 kernel fusion moves 52 to 62 tokens/s before quantization gives 3.1× more. Falcon-7B's official implementation did not support the KV cache correctly. Speedup over llama.cpp on Orin is at most 1.7×.

caveats: The comparison to other systems shows smaller gains of 1.2-3.0×
Raspberry Pi 4B reaches only 0.7 tokens/s for 7B models

findings.claim: Using smaller (64KB–256KB) pages requires modifying the open-source NVIDIA unified-memory driver, because the closed-source CUDA VMM APIs only allocate in multiples of 2MB. This limits portability and deployability.
findings.mechanism: cuMemCreate supports only 2MB granularity and lives in closed-source drivers. Fine-grained pages therefore depend on custom driver APIs (vMem*) built on cudaMallocManaged. Without them, 2MB pages cause internal fragmentation, which limits batch size.
conditions: Fine-grained page sizes below 2MB are needed
Stock NVIDIA drivers are used without the authors' modifications
Environments where custom kernel-driver changes are not allowed or maintainable

evidence.support_description: CUDA VMM APIs are closed-source and support only 2MB pages, so the authors implemented new APIs in the open-source driver.
Their driver changes extend unified memory (cudaMallocManaged), which allocates 2MB pages by default and can cause severe fragmentation.

caveats: Tensor slicing offers a driver-free alternative that cuts fragmentation to 1/N
Tensor slicing makes per-layer KV non-contiguous and needs kernels with stride support; earlier FlashInfer lacked this
The paper does not evaluate end-to-end performance with tensor slicing

findings.claim: With 2MB pages, the default granularity for stock CUDA VMM, vAttention suffers more internal fragmentation and supports smaller maximum batch sizes than with 64KB pages.
findings.mechanism: A 2MB page-group holds thousands of tokens per layer-tensor (e.g., 1024–4096 tokens). Per-request allocation granularity is therefore coarse, and partially filled pages waste memory.
conditions: 2MB page-groups
Throughput-oriented workloads with large batch sizes that are memory-bound

evidence.support_description: 2MB pages served max batch sizes of 187/203/56 versus 240/258/68 for 64KB pages on Yi-6B/Llama-3-8B/Yi-34B.

caveats: The authors state 2MB pages are good enough for many online serving scenarios with latency constraints

findings.claim: vAttention depends on hiding the high latency of CUDA VMM API calls with background threads and deferred reclamation. When these are not applicable or fail to cover the cost, allocation adds noticeable latency.
findings.mechanism: Each map or unmap call costs tens of microseconds and involves an OS-kernel round trip. Growing one Yi-34B request takes about 5ms, scaling with the number of requests needing pages. Overlapping works only because decode memory demand is predictable and iterations are long. Prefill relies on reuse of a previous request's pages or on eager allocation.
conditions: Synchronous allocation, i.e. without the optimizations
Prefill when no cached or eagerly mapped pages are available
Short iterations or many requests needing new pages simultaneously

evidence.support_description: Synchronous allocation causes latency spikes of 5–15 ms per decode iteration and prefill overhead of up to 1.15× with 64KB pages.

caveats: Overheads were shown to be hidden in the tested configurations
Memory pressure that forces reclamation or the 10% threshold was not studied in detail

findings.claim: Virtual-memory pre-reservation assumes abundant virtual address space and sizes the buffers for the maximum batch size and maximum context length, which may limit configurations with very large B, L, or number of layers.
findings.mechanism: Reserving 2×N buffers of size B×S per worker requires large virtual address ranges (e.g., 12TB for Yi-34B with B=500). This is argued to be fine within 128TB of user-addressable space, but the margin shrinks as B, L, and N grow.
conditions: Very large maximum batch size or context length
Many layers per worker
Workers with limited user-addressable virtual space

evidence.support_description: Pre-reserves virtual memory assuming every request has maximum context length. Example: 120 buffers of 100GB each (12TB).

caveats: The paper argues virtual memory is plentiful
The paper does not test extreme configurations

findings.claim: The design relies on kernel support for batch indexing (cache_batch_idx) to handle holes from continuous batching, and each request is bound to a fixed reqId slot. This limits support for attention kernels lacking such flexibility.
findings.mechanism: Requests occupy fixed sub-regions of the virtual tensor at offsets reqId×S, so exits leave holes. Handling these requires kernels that let Q and the KV cache differ in batch size and order. Kernels without this feature would need changes.
conditions: Attention kernels without cache_batch_idx-like arguments
Continuous batching
caveats: FlashAttention provides this API
The paper does not enumerate which other kernels meet this requirement

findings.claim: vAttention provides no decode-throughput advantage over the best PagedAttention kernel; its gains are concentrated in prefill-heavy, long-context workloads. Benefits shrink for short contexts and low prefill:decode ratios.
findings.mechanism: Decode attention is memory-bound, so paging's extra compute is hidden. For short contexts, linear operators dominate prefill cost. The benefit of faster non-paged kernels therefore shows only when prefill attention is a significant share of runtime.
conditions: Decode-dominated workloads
Short contexts (below roughly 16K)
Low P:D ratio

evidence.support_description: FA2_vAttention is on par with FA2_Paged in decode. Throughput is nearly identical for small contexts. Gains are proportional to context length and P:D ratio.

caveats: Much of the decode gain over vLLM stems from vLLM's slower kernel, not from the memory approach itself

findings.claim: The evaluation is narrow: a single serving framework (vLLM v0.2.7), A100/H100 GPUs, three models, mostly long-context offline or online workloads, and a limited set of attention kernels. Generalization and fairness are therefore uncertain.
findings.mechanism: Results depend on the integration with an old vLLM version and specific kernel versions. Baseline configurations were hand-tuned. Some alternatives were omitted from evaluation, e.g. FlashInfer's non-paged decode kernel, which is up to 14.6× slower. FA3 was compared only with FA2, since it has no paged counterpart.
conditions: Other serving frameworks, GPUs, or model architectures
Short-context or mixed workloads
Newer vLLM/kernel versions that reduce paging overheads

evidence.support_description: Single framework version, three models, FlashInfer non-paged decode omitted, FA3 not compared with a paged equivalent.

caveats: Authors report consistent results for page-size effects on Llama-3-70B and GPT-3-175B in a separate experiment
Artifact is released to reproduce results

findings.claim: vAttention does not provide mechanisms for swapping KV cache to CPU, and handling of memory exhaustion is limited to preemption. Other features, such as prefix sharing, are only discussed rather than demonstrated.
findings.mechanism: The step API returns failure when memory demand cannot be met, and the framework preempts requests. More sophisticated policies are deferred to future work. Prefix de-duplication is discussed only in the context of unified-memory limitations.
conditions: Memory-oversubscribed deployments
Workloads with shared prefixes

evidence.support_description: The authors leave swapping KV cache to CPU as future work.

caveats: Preemption matches vLLM's default behavior

findings.claim: The no-TLB-thrashing conclusion for 64KB pages is established only for attention kernels with regular access patterns and on specific GPUs, and is attributed to hand-tuned implementations without a detailed mechanism.
findings.mechanism: The paper observes no slowdown with 64KB versus 2MB pages and attributes this to the regular computation pattern and hand-tuned kernels avoiding irregular accesses, without a direct TLB-level analysis.
conditions: Irregular or newly designed attention kernels
Different GPU architectures

evidence.support_description: Runtime differences are within about 2% for prefill and decode on Llama-3-8B; the explanation is stated as 'we attribute this to...'.

caveats: Reported consistent for larger models in a separate experiment
